abstract: The integration of light-programmable valley optoelectronic nanocircuits based on two-dimensional semiconductors has been limited by complex optical readout using bulk optics. Now, a chip integrates a metasurface with a waveguide and on-chip photodetectors to generate, sort, and read out optical valley signals in the near field, all at room temperature.

title: Methods, trade-offs and opportunities in high-speed optical microscopy for neural voltage imaging
abstract: Electrical signals in neurons underlie perception, movement, memory and behaviour, yet many unfold too rapidly to be captured by conventional optical imaging. Calcium imaging has transformed neuroscience but provides an indirect and relatively slow readout of electrical activity. By directly measuring membrane potential changes, voltage imaging enables millisecond-scale recording of action potentials, subthreshold dynamics and signal propagation across neural circuits. Recent advances in voltage-sensitive dyes and genetically encoded voltage indicators have made voltage imaging increasingly practical, motivating the development of fluorescence microscopy methods optimized for high-speed acquisition. However, voltage imaging remains constrained by trade-offs among imaging speed, spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratios and photodamage. In this Review we discuss high-speed optical microscopy strategies that address these challenges and highlight the need for co-design among voltage indicators, imaging systems and computational analysis.

title: Laser–plasma amplification of an ultrabroadband laser pulse to 0.3 TW
abstract: Producing on-target laser intensities much greater than 10 23 W cm − 2 with current laser technologies is a roadblock to accessing new regimes of physics such as strong-field quantum electrodynamics. Laser–plasma amplifiers show promise to realize these intensities by augmenting the final amplifier and compressor in traditional chirped-pulse-amplification architectures with a plasma-based amplification and compression stage that operates at a much higher damage threshold. Here we demonstrate amplification of an ultrabroadband (>60 nm) pulse in a laser–plasma Raman amplifier. We directly amplified seed intensities up to 3.7 × 10 15 W cm − 2 and measured efficiencies up to 8.7%. Single-shot SPIDER measurements show a factor-of-2 reduction in the amplified pulse duration with final powers up to 0.3 TW, a 10× improvement over previous results. Final pulse durations of 64 fs are measured. Energy transfers greater than 220 mJ from the picosecond pump into the seed result in a 30× energy amplification of a 7.6 mJ seed. These results set the stage for a compact plasma afterburner based on Raman amplification that could extend the scientific capability of existing petawatt-class laser facilities to enable experiments at the intensity frontier.

title: Correlated electrons extend X-ray high-harmonic generation beyond the single-electron limit
abstract: High-harmonic generation underpins attosecond science. For over three decades, high-harmonic upconversion has been framed within the confines of a single-active-electron light–matter interaction featuring a well-defined cutoff photon energy. Here we demonstrate experimentally that correlated electrons can propel high-harmonic emission beyond this single-active-electron limit, markedly increasing the generated photon energies. We observe a weak secondary plateau that extends the conventional cutoff beyond 120 eV up to the water window at 280 eV. This phenomenon arises from double-electron recombination of strongly correlated electron pairs, resulting in a new cutoff scaling of up to 5.5 times the ponderomotive energy of the rescattering electrons, which notably deviates from the conventional scaling factor of 3.2. These findings reshape our fundamental understanding of the high-harmonic upconversion process and position high-harmonic generation as a potent photonic probe of attosecond-to-femtosecond electron correlations in quantum systems, opening new pathways for advanced ultrafast spectroscopy, novel attosecond source development and the exploration of strongly correlated quantum materials.

title: Integrated optical isolators for broadband multi-laser operation
abstract: Photonic integrated circuits commonly feature visible or near-infrared lasers that are vulnerable to destabilizing back-reflections and must be protected by isolators—non-reciprocal optical components enforcing one-way light propagation. Despite recent progress, high-performance isolators remain bulky off-chip components, while on-chip implementations suffer from challenging fabrication, high optical absorption or narrow optical bandwidth. Here we propose and experimentally demonstrate a magnet-free, intrinsically broadband travelling-wave isolator built from foundry-compatible components. Using radio-frequency electro-optic modulation to create synthetic motion across four parallel waveguides, we realize dynamic rotating destructive interference that continuously cancels backward-propagating light while leaving forward-propagating light unaffected. We reach ~30 dB peak isolation, maintain >24 dB isolation across a 30-nm-wavelength span with thermo-optic adjustment and show >20 dB isolation for two lasers simultaneously within 10 nm without any adjustment. The demonstration’s 770–800-nm-wavelength span covers key alkali atomic transitions, enabling on-chip laser isolation for atomic spectroscopy, laser cooling and locking applications. Our isolator approach, applicable from the visible to telecom wavelength spectrum, offers a compelling practical solution, opening the way for fully integrated atomic clocks, quantum sensors, advanced telecommunications and tunable laser systems on a single chip.

title: X-ray-driven Hanbury Brown and Twiss spectroscopy
abstract: Hanbury Brown and Twiss interferometry was a milestone experiment that transformed our understanding of the nature of light. Originally demonstrated in 1956 to measure the radii of stars through photon-correlation detection, it later became a cornerstone of modern quantum optics. Here we connect Hanbury Brown and Twiss interferometry to the physics of scintillation, the process of spontaneous light emission upon excitation by high-energy particles, such as X-rays. By revealing the underlying photon bunching in the scintillation process, we use the photon correlations \({g}^{\left(2\right)}\left(\tau \right)\) to quantify the intrinsic light emission properties of the scintillator, specifically the emission time and the number of optical photons emitted per X-ray photon. This approach provides a characterization method that we benchmark on a wide gamut of scintillators, including several rare-earth-doped (and undoped) oxide single-crystal scintillators and perovskite nanocrystals, thereby showing the dependence of their properties on temperature and X-ray flux. Our method is particularly important for nano- and microscale scintillators, whose properties are challenging to quantify by conventional means. We extract the scintillation properties even in quantum-dot superlattices of only a few hundreds of nanometres and observed strong photon bunching ( \({g}^{\left(2\right)}\left(0\right) > 50\) ). Our research paves the way for the broader use of methods from quantum optics for studying materials with complex optical properties in extreme regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.

title: Cold-atom comagnetometry via optical control of spin states
abstract: Atomic-spin-based comagnetometers are powerful tools for precision sensing and tests of fundamental physics. Compared with the widely used gas-cell comagnetometer systems, cold-atom systems offer access to much shorter distance scales and allow the implementation of optical quantum control techniques. However, to realize long spin coherence times with cold atoms, it is necessary to use diamagnetic atoms and overcome decoherence induced by light shifts. Here we demonstrate a cold-atom comagnetometer based on the nuclear spins of 171 Yb (spin-1/2) and 173 Yb (spin-5/2), jointly trapped in an optical lattice. Vector light shifts are suppressed by enforcing linear polarization of the lattice, whereas tensor shifts in 173 Yb are suppressed via the use of a Schrödinger cat state. This enables simultaneous Ramsey interferometry on both isotopes with a spin coherence time of 60 s. We achieve a magnetic noise suppression factor exceeding 3 × 10 4 , and determine the 171 Yb– 173 Yb ratio of nuclear magnetic moments to be –0.726076(3) with a 4-ppm precision. Our results establish a new cold-atom platform for spin-based sensing and open pathways towards quantum-enhanced searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

title: Edge-on perovskite detectors with suppressed shallow traps for counting X-ray photons at medical computed tomography fluxes
abstract: Metal halide perovskite semiconductors are becoming promising candidates for X-ray photon-counting detectors due to their combination of strong stopping power, excellent electronic properties and low cost. However, a key challenge for semiconductor photon-counting computed tomography detectors is that existing response speeds are insufficient to count high-flux X-ray photons at a rate of 3 × 10 6 –1 × 10 8 photons per second per square millimetre (s −1 mm −2 ) in common computed tomography scanning. Here we report a combination of edge-on device configuration and chloride alloying to increase the response speed of perovskite photon-counting detectors. The edge-on configuration shortens the charge collection distance by 15 times while maintaining the X-ray absorption, reducing charge transit time by 225 times. Surprisingly, we find that free charges generated by nearly every incident X-ray photon encounter shallow traps in formamidinium lead bromide (FAPbBr 3 ) crystal devices. Chloride alloying of FAPbBr 3 crystals dramatically reduces shallow trap density, increasing detector response speed. The high electric field in the edge-on detectors enables complete extraction of charges even if they are trapped by shallow defects. The resulting perovskite detectors show a response time of 37 ns after deconvolution. The edge-on detectors with a pixel size of 200 × 200 µm 2 can count 120-kVp X-ray photons, with a high flux of 2 × 10 8 photons s −1 mm −2 , enabling the application of perovskite photon-counting detectors for photon-counting computed tomography and many other applications.

title: Ultrafast electron diffraction with MeV electron source from a laser wakefield accelerator
abstract: MeV ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) is a widely used technique for ultrafast structural dynamics studies of matter in numerous areas. The development of the laser wakefield accelerator (LWFA) shows great potential for an advanced all-optical electron source based on LWFA in UED applications. Here we experimentally demonstrated that an LWFA-based device with a miniaturized permanent magnet beamline can generate and manipulate electron beams suitable for UED. During beam transport, the LWFA electron beams with intrinsically short duration undergo temporal stretching owing to the energy spread and are subsequently compressed by the following double-bend achromat. The optimized double-bend achromat can make the beamline isochronous such that the arrival time jitter induced by the shot-to-shot energy fluctuation can be eliminated, and allow the advantage of the natural laser-beam synchronization for LWFAs to emerge. With the energy filtering, the beam energy spread can be reduced to 3% (full-width at half-maximum), while a sufficient amount of charge (11.9 fC) per bunch for diffraction is retained. Using a laser-driven terahertz deflector, the beam length and arrival time jitter measured at the sample location are approximately 49.6 fs (root mean square (r.m.s.)) and 4.7 fs (r.m.s.), respectively, resulting in a temporal resolution of ~49.8 fs. Comprehensive start-to-end simulations indicate the potential of reducing the bunch length to ~10 fs (r.m.s.) with a lower energy spread of around 1.6%. Clear single-shot and multi-shot diffraction patterns of single-crystalline gold samples are obtained, and the derived lattice constant agrees well with the actual value. Our proof-of-principle experiments open the door to the detection of ultrafast structural dynamics using MeV LWFA beams, and pave the way for UED applications with sub-10 fs temporal resolution.

title: In situ dry repair and passivation unlocks size-independent performance in Ⅲ-nitride micro-LEDs
abstract: Nitride-based micro-LEDs are poised to revolutionize next-generation displays with exceptional brightness and contrast, but their efficiency collapses at the micrometre scale owing to etching-induced sidewall damage, a critical bottleneck hindering commercialization. Here we introduce an in situ dry repair and passivation (IDRP) technique that effectively eliminates plasma-induced sidewall damage, unlocking the full potential of micro-scale devices. This approach not only substantially overcomes the size-related efficiency degradation but also enables a reversed size effect, where efficiency increases as dimensions shrink, even down to 1.6 μm devices. The IDRP-treated devices also exhibit substantially improved manufacturing yield and electrostatic discharge robustness. The IDRP strategy proves universally effective across the nitride-based spectrum, leading to record-high peak external quantum efficiencies of 64.7% and 55.1% for 2 μm blue and green InGaN micro-LEDs, respectively. These unprecedented performance metrics enable high-performance pixels, demonstrated here in a nitride microdisplay tailored for emerging augmented reality and virtual reality applications. As a fully integrated, semiconductor-standard dry process, IDRP provides a simple, rapid and powerful route to advance the industrialization of micro-LEDs, representing a transformative technology for large-scale display manufacturing.

title: Ultra-wideband electrically tuned mid-infrared on-chip parametric oscillator
abstract: Developing compact, broadband mid-infrared coherent sources for applications in spectroscopy and sensing remains a pressing challenge in photonics. However, material limitations and integration constraints have restricted the accessible wavelengths and operation bandwidths of current mid-infrared lasers. Here we address these challenges by developing a nonlinear integrated photonic device that converts a fixed-wavelength near-infrared pump laser into broadly tunable mid-infrared light. Our device, an optical parametric oscillator integrated on thin-film lithium niobate, generates 22 THz of multi-milliwatt, voltage-tunable radiation from 2.7 to 3.4 μm, a region typically difficult to access but vital for environmental, chemical and biological sensing. By introducing an on-chip-tunable parametric oscillator architecture taking advantage of the Vernier effect, we obtain electrical control of the emission wavelengths from coarse, multi-terahertz scales down to continuous, sub-100-GHz mode-hop-free tuning ranges. This work establishes a robust platform for a new class of compact, widely tunable mid-infrared sources with potential for future scaling.

title: Fluid motion and crystallization control enable air-processed fully screen-printed perovskite solar cells
abstract: Fully screen-printed perovskite solar cells represent a promising solution for scalable manufacturing of perovskite photovoltaics. However, their development is hindered by inefficient vertical phase transformation within thick, multi-layered films, which results in incomplete infiltration, premature surface nucleation and residual stress. Here we report a fluid motion crystallization strategy employing a co-solvent system of ionic liquid methylammonium propionate and butyronitrile. The butyronitrile reduces the fluid motion resistance and disperses PbI 2 aggregates with optimized solvation structure, enabling rapid and deep infiltration of the perovskite precursor. This promotes a bottom-up, ordered phase transition before surface nucleation, effectively suppressing defect formation. The subsequent growth of a dense, interconnected perovskite nanocrystal network featuring an island-like surface morphology strengthens the interfacial contact with the carbon electrode. This intimate contact enhances the carrier transport and minimizes the recombination losses. Finally, air-processed, fully screen-printed perovskite solar cells yield a power conversion efficiency of 22.41% (certified 21.86%). Devices retain over 90.5% of their initial power conversion efficiency after 2,000 h under International Summit on Organic Photovoltaic Stability light-soaking-1 (ISOS-L-1) accelerated ageing conditions and show no degradation after 900 h of operation at 85 °C with 50% ± 10% relative humidity (ISOS-L-3 protocol).

title: Time to embrace new platforms
abstract: With silicon-based integrated photonics having reached commercial-level maturity, the research community is directing its efforts towards heterogeneous designs and alternative material platforms with new functionalities.

title: Plasma mirror self-focusing boosts gamma-ray generation
abstract: One approach to generate high-energy X-rays and γ-rays is inverse Compton scattering, where a high-energy electron beam collides with an intense laser pulse. However, this process is notoriously difficult because the electron and laser beams must be precisely aligned in space and time. Now, a coated plasma mirror is shown to dramatically increase the efficiency and energy of the generation.

title: A milestone toward exawatt plasma optics by Raman amplification
abstract: Exawatt-to-zettawatt lasers are essential in the quest for an ultimate understanding of nature, but they are held back by the damage limits of conventional optics. A recent experiment of Raman pulse compression to terawatt power revitalizes the prospect of plasma-based optics for next-generation ultraintense lasers.

title: The state and prospects of the European photonics sector
abstract: At the centre of Europe’s rich photonics ecosystem, the European Photonics Industry Consortium (EPIC) connects stakeholders and promotes collective actions and advocacy. Nature Photonics spoke to its Director General Carlos Lee about recent trends, strengths and challenges facing Europe.

title: Mechanochromic tactile sensing
Doped germanium keeps pace with the light field
abstract: Attosecond transient reflection spectroscopy reveals that doped germanium can retain a light-field-driven sub-cycle optical response, with impurity doping shifting and reshaping electron dynamics on attosecond timescales.

title: Optical hydrogen sensing across scales
abstract: An optofluidic microcavity combined with an adaptive laser-locking scheme makes it possible to monitor hydrogen from individual molecules to per cent-level concentrations with a compact device.

title: All-organic polymer with large refractive index in the near-infrared
abstract: Organic polymers that are highly transparent, ductile and lightweight are very attractive for optical applications. However, at present, the capabilities of all-organic polymers lag far behind their inorganic analogues due to their lower refractive index ( n ) ( n ≈ 1.4–1.6) and poor infrared transparency. Here we report a high-refractive-index ( n ≈ 2.53 at 750 nm) all-organic polymer (K153) with unique cyano substitutions, which possesses a much higher refractive index than inorganic chalcogenide glasses and CdS/ZnS/ZnSe (>2.25). Moreover, K153 exhibits outstanding infrared transparency, owing to the symmetric architectures of constructing units that reduce infrared light losses. The underlying mechanism behind the high n value of K153 is attributed to its larger polarization and enhanced intermolecular interactions induced by linear cyano groups. Furthermore, superiorities of K153 films including impressive environmental tolerance, opportunities for high-quality infrared imaging, extraordinary flexibility, tunable n values via chemical doping and nanoimprint ability were also demonstrated. The results not only provide a very competitive n for infrared-transparent organic polymers over inorganic materials but also demonstrate that tailored cyano engineering can optimize the molecular structure effectively, culminating in a dramatic increase in n and a step towards the use of all-organic polymers for infrared applications.

title: Integrated electro-optic circulator on thin-film lithium niobate for bidirectional optical fibre transmission
abstract: Optical circulators are a key component for optical systems, routing light between ports to manage signal flow and protect components from back-reflection. As integrated photonics advances towards chip-scale systems, incorporating key optical building blocks on chip is increasingly important. Optical circulators have been slow to follow this process. Although conventional circulators break Lorentz reciprocity using magneto-optic materials, they are impractical to integrate into devices. Here we realize a broadband electro-optic travelling-wave optical circulator based on thin-film lithium niobate that achieves non-reciprocity without magnetic materials, resonant structures or wavelength conversion. Our architecture uses cascaded travelling-wave Mach–Zehnder modulators driven by electrical sinusoidal signals, achieving up to 37 dB peak isolation, spanning the full O- and C+L optical telecom bands (14 THz bandwidth). The device shows excess losses of 0.1 dB (port 1 to 2) and 4.9 dB (port 2 to 3), with 0.84 dB of passive losses. To demonstrate practicality, we deploy this circulator in same-wavelength, bidirectional coherent transmission, achieving 400G/polarization with industry-compliant hardware, digital signal processing and forward-error-correction codes. These results establish a scalable route to broadband on-chip circulation, with relevance to industry-standard optical fibre transmission systems and position electro-optic non-reciprocity as a manufacturable, foundry-compatible building block for the next generation of integrated optical transceivers.

title: On-chip space–time wave packet laser array
abstract: Harnessing the full dimensionality of light by coupling its spatial and temporal degrees of freedom offers a powerful means to engineer optical fields with diverse functionalities. Such space–time structured light fields—ranging from localized wave packets to spatiotemporal vortices—hold promise for transforming ultrafast science, laser machining, imaging and optical communications. However, their realization has so far relied on complex free-space configurations, requiring bulky components such as gratings and spatial light modulators placed in Fourier-conjugate planes. Here we introduce a chip-scale platform that generates space–time wave packets directly from a laser array, bridging the gap between structured light physics and integrated photonics. Our design uses distributed feedback lasers with dual-ended geometries that produce mutually coherent sub-beams with stable phase contrasts. This versatile architecture enables precise control of spatial–spectral correlations, allowing the synthesis of incoherent or coherent space–time wave packets with scalable width and propagation length. By uniting field structuring and lasing within a single device, this approach opens a pathway towards integrated light sources capable of on-chip beam shaping, combining and spatiotemporal control, with far-reaching implications in microscopy, tomography, communications and ultrafast optical technologies.

title: Scalable and conformal nickel oxide for efficient perovskite solar modules
abstract: Scalable, conformal nickel oxide (NiO x ) is essential for uniform charge extraction in large-area inverted perovskite modules, yet traditional deposition comes with a trade-off between structural coverage and surface reactivity. Here we report a coordination-regulated strategy based on chemical bath deposition that resolves this bottleneck by governing the NiO x crystallization kinetics. By leveraging the high thermodynamic stability of Ni 2+ –potassium tartrate (Pta) complexes, we suppress disorderly aggregation and halve the hydrolysis rate constant to 0.124 l mol −1 min −1 . This precise kinetic control yields dense and conformal films with refined 4.8-nm nanocrystallites. This nanostructural refinement maximizes the surface density of hydroxyl groups, providing robust anchoring sites where self-assembled monolayers can form a chemically cohesive and defect-suppressed buried interface. Our Pta-NiO x strategy delivers inverted devices with a champion power conversion efficiency of 27.40% (certified reverse-scan power conversion efficiency of 27.35%) and module efficiencies of 23.42% (17.7 cm 2 ) and 21.97% (81.5 cm 2 ). Small-area devices retained 90% of their initial power conversion efficiency after 2,656 h, and 17.7 cm 2 mini-modules retained over 90% after 1,200 h under the ISOS-L-1I protocol.

title: Photonic accelerators for AI across cloud and edge platforms
abstract: Light-driven computing systems are closing the gap with state-of-the-art digital accelerators in terms of energy efficiency, compute throughput, density and latency. Here we map where photonic accelerators can matter in modern artificial intelligence infrastructure, and what must change for their impact at scale. We distinguish cloud-oriented, general-purpose photonic accelerators from application-specific, edge-oriented systems. In the cloud, the central challenge is scalability under tight energy budgets: heterogeneous systems with large vector inputs suffer from losses and electro–optic interfaces that dominate power and impede throughput, preventing the commercial deployment of photonic tensor cores. At the edge, opportunities arise wherever ultralow latency or high spatial parallelism are required and tight energy constraints dominate—for instance, in on-fibre optical processing and vision—yet progress is limited by the underwhelming scalability of all-optical nonlinearities, the lack of efficient reconfigurability, and a sizable optics footprint. We conclude that photonics is a viable near-term strategy within the existing digital ecosystem, and with focused advances along these axes, it can enable more sustainable artificial intelligence and open the door to broader adoption over the next decade.

title: Inverted phosphorescent OLEDs with plasmon coupling from quantum dot interlayers for enhanced efficiency
abstract: The efficiency and operational stability of phosphorescent organic light-emitting diodes are fundamentally limited by photonic losses arising from waveguide and surface plasmon polariton modes. Here we introduce a colloidal quantum dot (QD) interlayer as a plasmonic coupling medium in an inverted phosphorescent organic light-emitting diode architecture to mitigate these losses. Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements reveal an efficient plasmonic coupling between the emissive layer and the QD interlayer, enabling the recovery of energy that would otherwise be dissipated through surface plasmon polariton modes. Three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations further demonstrate that the QD interlayer modifies the local density of optical states, redistributes the trapped optical energy and enhances outcoupling into air modes. Quantitative analysis indicates that the QD interlayer intercepts approximately 30.7% of the energy initially coupled to surface plasmon polariton modes. Consequently, the QD-integrated inverted phosphorescent organic light-emitting diode achieves an external quantum efficiency of 20.95%, representing a 1.3-fold improvement over the reference device (15.67%). These findings establish QD interlayers as an effective and versatile strategy for suppressing plasmonic losses and improving light extraction in high-performance OLEDs.

title: Volumetrically continuous 3D dynamic holography via cascaded light-field propagation
abstract: True-to-life three-dimensional (3D) video display via computer-generated holography is highly sought-after in virtual reality, augmented reality and human–computer interactions. However, high crosstalk fundamentally limits 3D projection continuity. Most methods reconstruct 3D scenes by stacking widely spaced axial or lateral planes, yielding discontinuous reconstructions that diminish the realism. State-of-the-art techniques still balance crosstalk against plane spacing, preventing fully continuous 3D projection. Here we propose a holistic design paradigm based on a cascaded light-field propagation mechanism that reuses outgoing light as constructive input for subsequent planes, thereby transforming the crosstalk into a useful signal. To address the computational challenges associated with our method, we develop a physics-embedded, untrained holographic diffractive prior neural network framework (Holo-Prior-Net) that serves as a computational realization tool. Without pretraining, it can efficiently design 3D holograms through its architectural prior. We demonstrate free-space 3D light-field projection that is both axially and laterally continuous using a spatial light modulator. Beyond volume-rendered reconstructions, the 3D continuity is directly observable across wide range of viewing angles, confirming the physical realization. By reconstructing the underlying design logic rather than incrementally improving image metrics, this work provides an alternative route towards projecting volumetrically continuous 3D objects.

title: Millimetre-wave generation with 18 zs Hz−1/2 timing noise floor via Kerr optical frequency division
abstract: Millimetre-wave oscillators are essential for communication, radar, spectroscopy and emerging photonic–electronic systems, yet their spectral purity remains constrained by noise processes intrinsic to direct generation at the carrier frequency. Here we demonstrate a fundamentally different approach that circumvents these limits by optically dividing a multiterahertz reference to the millimetre-wave domain using Kerr soliton dynamics. A 3.3-THz dual-wavelength Brillouin laser injection-locks a chip-scale Kerr microcomb, enforcing exact optical frequency division to a 300-GHz repetition rate without electronic multiplication or feedback control. The resulting oscillator enters a previously inaccessible noise regime, exhibiting single-sideband phase noise of −152 dBc Hz −1 at a 1-MHz offset, corresponding to an unprecedented timing noise floor of 18 zs Hz −1/2 for a directly photodetected microwave or millimetre-wave signal. Integration of the measured phase-noise spectrum from 1 kHz to 1 MHz yields a root-mean-square timing jitter of 135 attoseconds. To directly resolve this performance, we implement cross-correlation phase-noise metrology at 300 GHz using independent photonic local oscillators. These results establish Kerr optical frequency division as a general and scalable route to millimetre-wave and subterahertz carriers whose coherence is no longer constrained by direct-generation limits, opening a new operating regime for photonic oscillators.

title: Observation of multiphoton entanglement in resonance fluorescence
abstract: Resonance fluorescence, the process in which a single two-level quantum emitter interacts with a near-resonant coherent light, is a cornerstone of quantum optics as a paradigmatic light–matter interaction. Quantum phenomena in resonance fluorescence have been accounted for in terms of one- and two-photon processes; however, the physical processes arising from the interaction of a single two-level atom with higher photon numbers remain unexplored experimentally. Here we experimentally reveal the multiphoton scattering nature of resonance fluorescence, which intrinsically gives rise to multiphoton entanglement. By accessing quantum fluctuations in the field emitted from a cavity quantum electrodynamics system, we resolve third- and fourth-order photon scattering events from a single two-level atom. In the three-photon component, the scattered photons are shown to be genuinely energy–time entangled, as verified by a violation of Svetlichny’s inequality. As a demonstration of an application, a quantum secret sharing protocol is implemented using this entangled photon source. Our study refines the descriptive framework of resonance fluorescence and broadens the scope of its investigation. It also establishes a fundamentally simple route for generating multiphoton entangled states for quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

title: Attosecond streaking of photoelectron angular momentum
abstract: Electric field E( t ) and the associated vector potential A( t ) are two important physical quantities that describe a light wave. Attosecond streaking measures the vector potential by mapping it onto photoelectron energy shifts, providing a largely classical picture of continuum-electron dynamics. Here we introduce angle-resolved attosecond streaking and combine experiment with time-dependent Schrödinger equation and strong-field approximation calculations to access the evolution of continuum-electron partial waves. We find that more partial waves are populated near the electric-field crest than near the vector-potential crest, whereas the dominant interference evolves from same-parity to opposite-parity channels. The analysis further reveals substantial multiphoton continuum–continuum coupling even at weak infrared light intensities. These results establish a quantum-state-resolved picture of attosecond streaking and provide a new insight into its non-perturbative nature.

title: Programmable photonic unitary processor enables parameterized differentiable long-haul spatial division multiplexed transmission
abstract: The explosive growth of global data traffic demands scalable and energy-efficient optical communication systems. Spatial division multiplexing (SDM) using multicore or multimode fibres is a promising solution to overcome the capacity limit of single-mode fibres. However, long-haul SDM transmission faces substantial challenges due to modal dispersion, which imposes heavy computational loads on digital signal processing for signal equalization. Here we propose parameterized SDM transmission, where programmable photonic unitary processors are installed at intermediate nodes. Instead of relying on conventional digital equalization on only the receiver side, our approach enables direct optimization of the SDM transmission channel itself by the programmable unitary processor, which reduces digital post-processing loads. We introduce a gradient-based optimization algorithm using a differentiable SDM transmission model to determine the optimal unitary transformation. Using this approach, we implement a telecom-grade programmable photonic unitary processor for low-loss, wideband (full C band), polarization-independent and high-fidelity ( R 2 > 96% across the C band) operation and experimentally report 1,300-km transmission using a three-mode fibre. The optimized photonic processor substantially reduces modal dispersion and post-processing complexity. Our results establish a scalable framework for integrating photonic computation into optical layers, enabling more efficient, high-capacity optical networks.

title: Dangling-bond-free, chemically anisotropic semiconductors for ultrahigh-resolution X-ray imaging
abstract: Interfacial defects, particularly those of intergranular origin, are a persistent challenge limiting the performance of modern optoelectronic devices. Conventional three-dimensional and low-dimensional (two- or one-dimensional) semiconductors all suffer from surface or edge-related bonding discontinuities that degrade the carrier dynamics and optical efficiency. Here we report on a new semiconductor design strategy based on zero-dimensional structured materials, which inherently lack dangling bonds along all crystallographic directions. By introducing anisotropic chemical bonding within the zero-dimensional framework, we can achieve customizable morphologies—such as rods—without compromising the isotropic and defect-free electronic properties. Using the uranyl-based halide Cs 2 UO 2 Cl 4 as a model, we exploit the bonding disparity between U=O and U–Cl to drive anisotropic crystal growth. When applied to X-ray scintillation imaging, columnar structured Cs 2 UO 2 Cl 4 achieved a high spatial resolution (34 lp mm −1 ). This work introduces a generalizable approach for decoupling material geometry and electronic dimensionality, offering a new platform for high-performance, defect-tolerant semiconductors.

title: Lattice light sheet activation structured illumination super-resolution microscopy
abstract: Volumetric super-resolution (SR) live imaging at high speed has been a long-standing challenge, especially in thick fluorescent specimens. Here we develop lattice light sheet activation structured illumination microscopy (LA-SIM), which integrates the advantages of superior optical sectioning and low phototoxicity offered by light sheet microscopy with SR-SIM in both linear and nonlinear schemes, using reversibly photoswitchable fluorescent protein. We also implement rationalized deep-learning denoising in a self-supervised manner, enabling high-quality three-dimensional SR images at limited signal-to-noise ratios, while achieving spatial resolution improvement beyond twofold relative to the diffraction limit in both lateral and axial dimensions (up to 87 nm and 203 nm, respectively). We utilize the high-quality rationalized deep-learning LA-SIM data to train a large-scale transformer model, SRFormer-pMoE, which overcomes the inferior properties and limited palette of reversibly photoswitchable fluorescent proteins. We show that the LA-SIM system syncretized with the SRFormer-pMoE model enables multicolour volumetric SR imaging from cultured cells to multicellular embryos, shedding new light on bioprocesses by tracking subcellular dynamics at high spatiotemporal resolution for durations of hours.

title: Endlessly self-injection-locked photonic integrated lasers
abstract: Narrow-linewidth integrated lasers are essential tools for optical atomic clocks, fibre sensing and other technologies. Recent advances in silicon nitride low-loss photonic integrated circuits allowed compact self-injection-locked semiconductor lasers to achieve exceptional coherence. Yet this architecture remains limited by sensitivity to detuning and feedback phase: narrow-linewidth operation occurs only at specific operating points, and maintaining the locked state requires active control, limiting robustness and hindering practical deployment. Here we demonstrate a photonic integrated turnkey self-injection-locked laser that eliminates these constraints, guaranteeing self-injection locking to a narrow-linewidth state at any drive current. Our approach exploits the feedback-phase dispersion, set by the spatial arrangement of resonator couplers—which governs the evolution of locking regimes across consecutive cavity modes. By engineering the feedback-phase dispersion and overlapping locking ranges in a high- Q silicon nitride photonic integrated microresonator, we constrain the laser to remain on narrow-linewidth branches during tuning, eliminating transitions into the free-running state. The photonic integrated laser exhibits persistent locking with intrinsic linewidths below 10 Hz at all drive currents, as well as during mode-hop-free 1.5-GHz frequency chirps enabled by monolithically integrated piezoelectric actuators. The architecture transforms the sensitive self-injection locking of low-loss photonic integrated circuits into a robust and scalable approach to ultralow-noise lasers.

title: Trans-interface engineering for reliable perovskite solar cells with reproducible stability
abstract: High reproducibility in interface-dominated device stability is crucial for the industrialization of perovskite solar cells. Conventional interface engineering uses planar interlayers to passivate and interlock the perovskite and the charge-transport layer, which often involves a trade-off between efficient charge transport and high stability. In this work, we use trans-interface engineering to create vertically aligned, mechanically tough nanolinks that penetrate both the perovskite and the charge-transport layer, simultaneously enhancing interface reliability and charge transfer. Here, as a proof of concept, we pre-incorporated triple and single organic linkers into the perovskite and the charge-transport layer, respectively, and then applied azobisisobutyronitrile-derived cyanoisopropyl radicals to trigger polymerization of the two linkers within their respective layers and to vertically bond them at the heterointerfacial contacts. A perovskite/charge-transport-layer interface enhanced by trans-interface engineering shows superior mechanical reliability compared with other reported interfacial approaches. The resultant perovskite solar cells deliver improved power conversion efficiencies of up to 27.04% (certified at 26.67%). Under maximum-power-point tracking at one-sun-intensity illumination, 92% of the tested perovskite solar cells reached T 80 lifetimes of 1,400 h, demonstrating improved stability and reproducibility. This high reliability stems largely from the trans-interface engineering-induced suppression of mechanical failure in device operation. This work points to a new direction for improving perovskite solar cells using trans-interfacial materials, which is also applicable to other multilayered optoelectronic devices beyond photovoltaics.

title: Giant phonon-assisted upconversion photoluminescence of in situ photo-carbonized polymer dots for 3D high-definition optical disks
abstract: Recent advancements in high-capacity storage technologies, especially solid-state drives, have made progress by employing multilevel encoding schemes that increase data density. In contrast, optical data storage systems face difficulties in achieving similar multilevel recording due to the limited dynamic range of photo-responsive materials and inherent signal-to-noise challenges. These material-level constraints limit optical encoding fidelity, preventing traditional optical platforms from achieving the rapid capacity growth seen in electronic storage. Here, to address these challenges, we present an approach utilizing giant anti-Stokes phonon-assisted upconversion photoluminescence via in situ laser writing and reading of upconversion carbonized polymer dots. This method enables high-capacity three-dimensional optical data storage with exceptional efficiency. Unlike conventional Stokes photoluminescence media, our approach maximizes near-infrared light utilization, achieving high resolution with ultralow noise. Our experimental demonstration showcases three-dimensional multilayer encoding with 1,024 distinct greyscale levels, reaching an estimated storage capacity of approximately 400 Tb on a DVD-sized disk while maintaining >99.99% reliability. Additionally, our methodology introduces a scalable pathway for extending greyscale encoding beyond 10,000 levels through optimized phonon–photon coupling, surpassing current petabit-scale optical storage capabilities and potentially laying the foundation for next-generation archival storage solutions with unprecedented density and fidelity.

title: Microchip Nd:YAG laser with master-oscillator–power-amplifier architecture
abstract: Diode-pumped solid-state lasers play a central role in modern photonics owing to their exceptional efficiency and ability to extend spectral coverage beyond the reach of semiconductor diodes. These attributes have enabled breakthroughs in precision metrology, quantum optics and coherent communications. However, bringing the proven advantages of diode-pumped solid-state gain media such as neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) onto an integrated photonic platform has remained difficult, largely due to inefficient pump utilization and limited power scaling in chip-scale implementations. Here we demonstrate a photonic-integrated Nd:YAG laser–amplifier system that overcomes these challenges with a microchip-based master-oscillator–power-amplifier architecture. The seed laser, employing a double-resonant microring resonator, could reach a threshold as low as 2.9 μW. The single-pass waveguide amplifier, when optimized separately, provides up to 46.6 dB small-signal gain. Combining the low-threshold seed with cascaded waveguide amplifiers, the integrated microchip-based master-oscillator–power-amplifier delivers more than 12 dBm of amplified continuous-wave output power. These results establish Nd:YAG waveguide integration as a practical route to compact and high-performance solid-state light sources.

title: Attosecond current control and timing in a scanning tunnelling microscope
abstract: Quantum tunnelling of electrons can be confined to the sub-cycle timescale of strong light fields, contributing decisively to the extreme time resolution of attosecond science. Because tunnelling also enables atomic-scale spatial resolution in scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), integrating STM with light pulses has long been a key objective in ultrafast microscopy, spanning the picosecond and femtosecond domains, with first signatures of attosecond dynamics. However, while sub-cycle dynamics on the attosecond timescale are routinely controlled and determined with high precision, controlling the direction of attosecond currents and determining their duration have remained elusive in STM. Here we induce STM tunnelling currents using two-colour laser pulses and dynamically control their direction, relying solely on the sub-cycle waveform of the pulses. Projecting our measurement data onto one-electron and many-body theory descriptions reveals a three-step transport process in the non-adiabatic tunnelling regime as the physical mechanism, with a theory-derived current burst duration of 860 as. Despite working under ambient conditions but free of thermal artefacts, we achieve sub-angström topographic sensitivity and a lateral spatial resolution of 2 nm. This unprecedented capability to directionally control attosecond bursts will enable the triggering and imaging of ultrafast charge dynamics at the spatiotemporal microscopy frontier of lightwave electronics.

title: Hybrid nanophotonic trap boosts atomic storage and coherence times
abstract: A hybrid nanophotonic trap that replaces the attractive red-detuned laser field with atom–surface interactions — Casimir–Polder interactions and electrostatic attraction — achieves record-long storage and coherence times for cold atoms coupled to a nanofibre surface.

title: Optomechanics for piconewton force metrology
abstract: Of the sensors that can directly sense forces in the pico- and sub-pico-newton ranges, only a few can measure in liquids. Microfibre-based microcantilevers now add to this family, providing a versatile, broad-bandwidth, high-sensitivity optomechanical sensor.

title: SHINE lights up the extremes
abstract: The Shanghai High Repetition Rate XFEL and Extreme Light Facility is approaching its first lasing. Nature Photonics spoke with Zhentang Zhao, director of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility and the SHINE project, about the facility’s capabilities and future plans.

title: Time-stretch spectroscopy breaks temporal aliasing barrier
abstract: A temporally super-resolved single-shot method overcomes the long-standing temporal–spectral trade-off in time-stretch spectroscopy. The outcome is continuous measurements of non-repetitive spectral dynamics with picosecond resolution, providing a three-orders-of-magnitude improvement over the current state of the art.

title: One super sensor from many
abstract: By combining 48 parallel sensors with diffractive multiplexing to recover information from the gaps between the sensors, a new wide-field microscope achieves a spatial resolution of approximately 3 micrometres over more than 5.2 square centimetres at 120 frames per second, substantially relaxing the conventional trade-off between field of view, resolution and imaging speed.

title: Delaying light from quantum dots
abstract: Förster energy transfer can prolong the photoluminescence decay of a receiving colloidal quantum dot, revealing a possible route to optically control recombination in nanocrystal assemblies.

title: Strong coupling of photon to an electron on helium
Phase control of interfering stimulated Raman pathways in the XUV regime
abstract: Coherent control uses interference between quantum pathways to enhance or suppress transitions to a target quantum state. In stimulated Raman excitation, such control can be achieved through interference between two indistinguishable pathways connecting the same initial and final states, with the relative phase between the pathways modulating the population transfer to the final state. Extending this strategy to the extreme ultraviolet (XUV) and X-ray regimes would enable control of ultrafast electronic dynamics and site-selective core excitations. However, Raman coupling at short wavelengths competes with photoionization and intermediate-state decay, whereas intense fields with stable and adjustable relative phases remain difficult to produce. Here we use two-colour pulses from a seeded coherent free-electron laser to excite helium from its ground state to a bound metastable state via stimulated XUV Raman excitation. We implement phase-coherent control by creating two interfering Raman pathways through the ionization continuum and modulate the transferred population by varying their relative phases. Blocking one pathway removes the modulation, confirming its interferometric origin, and time-dependent Schrödinger equation calculations reproduce the measured phase dependence. Our results establish phase-controlled stimulated Raman excitation in the XUV regime, providing a strategy for the coherent control of atomic and molecular processes at short wavelengths.

title: High-entropy molecular contacts enable high-efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells
abstract: The performance of inverted perovskite solar cells critically depends on the molecular contact formed by hole-selective self-assembled molecules. Conventional single-component hole-selective self-assembled molecules are prone to structural collapse under external stress, which disrupts hole transport and accelerates device degradation. Here we develop high-entropy molecular contacts (HE-MCs) by using a ternary blend of carbazole-naphthalene self-assembled molecules to simultaneously enhance device efficiency and operational stability. By blending molecules with similar chemical structures but distinct intermolecular interactions and packing motifs, we increase the packing-mode diversity to form a high-entropy system that affords efficient hole extraction and robust interfaces. Single-crystal analysis, molecular dynamics simulations and interfacial characterizations collectively confirm the successful formation of HE-MCs and their substantially improved resilience to external stress. Perovskite solar cells incorporating HE-MCs achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 27.50% (certified steady-state efficiency of 27.31%) and extended operational stability under various accelerated ageing tests, with negligible efficiency loss after 1,300 h under maximum power point tracking at 85 °C in ambient air. Our strategy provides a broadly applicable framework that exploits high entropy in packing modes for high-performance interfaces in perovskite photovoltaic devices.

title: Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes with reduced efficiency roll-off via accelerated exciton utilization
abstract: Efficiently harnessing all electrically generated excitons on a sufficiently fast timescale is essential for deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes to attain high efficiency, low roll-off and long operational lifetimes. Yet, this has constituted a long-standing challenge. Here we demonstrate deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes based on a dual-sensitizer emission system that enables multiple synergistic sensitization processes, achieving near-unity exciton utilization on a submicrosecond timescale. Our system features a blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence sensitizing host with a C 3 -symmetric triple donor–acceptor motif. Together, they create a cumulative effect from near-degenerate states that breaks the conventional trade-off between fast singlet radiation and efficient triplet upconversion. Such a design not only ensures efficient sensitization but also maintains the intrinsic narrowband emission of the final emitter. Our devices exhibit pure deep-blue emission with a chromaticity y -coordinate of 0.10 and a full width at half maximum of 15.4 nm. The maximum external quantum efficiency is 35.9%, 90% of which is maintained at an exceptionally high current density of 297.0 mA cm −2 . After 632 h of operation, the device luminance decreases to 80% of the initial 1,000 cd m −2 . Exciton dynamics studies reveal that the multiple sensitization pathways operating on a dominant submicrosecond timescale substantially suppress exciton annihilation, underpinning the remarkable device performance.

title: Solid-state emissive acceptors enable thermally accessible radiative pathways for efficient organic solar cells
abstract: Organic solar cells have achieved rapid efficiency improvements through the development of non-fullerene acceptors. However, non-radiative recombination through interfacial charge-transfer (CT) states remains one of the fundamental bottlenecks limiting further enhancement of open-circuit voltage and overall efficiency. In high-performance donor–acceptor blends, CT excitons formed at the interface exhibit weak radiative coupling and are prone to non-radiative decay, leading to suppressed electroluminescence and substantial voltage loss. Here we establish a thermally accessible radiative decay pathway enabled by a solid-state emissive guest acceptor strategy to suppress non-radiative CT recombination without compromising charge generation or transport. Incorporation of emissive Y-series acceptors into a state-of-the-art host system creates a localized excited (LE) state energetically resonant with the interfacial CT manifold. Experimental spectroscopies and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that interfacial CT excitons can thermally repopulate the LE state of the host acceptor and subsequently transfer to the emissive guest via efficient resonance energy transfer, establishing an indirect yet effective radiative recombination channel. As a result, devices exhibit markedly enhanced electroluminescence quantum efficiency and ultralow non-radiative voltage loss down to 0.142 eV while maintaining power conversion efficiencies of 17%. Single-junction ternary devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 21.2% (certified as 20.84%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.93 V. This work establishes solid-state luminescence-enabled CT–LE coupling as an effective photophysical strategy for minimizing energy loss in organic solar cells that is complementary to conventional morphology- or frontier-orbital energetic optimization.

title: Intermolecular decoupling of C60 suppresses interfacial recombination in perovskite solar cells
abstract: Interfacial non-radiative recombination, particularly at the C 60 electron-selective contact, remains a major bottleneck limiting the performance of inverted perovskite solar cells. While previous efforts have primarily focused on passivating trap states at the perovskite surface, the underlying mechanism by which fullerene-based electron transport layers induce interfacial recombination has remained unclear. Here we reveal that C 60 lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO)-derived band-like states arising from strong intermolecular coupling within the C 60 film drive recombination at the perovskite/C 60 interface. To mitigate this issue, we develop a vapour-phase molecular passivation strategy using trialkylamines to disrupt C 60 molecular packing, substantially weakening the C 60 LUMO-derived band-like states and suppressing interfacial non-radiative losses. The trialkylamine treatment minimizes the quasi-Fermi-level splitting loss after C 60 deposition from 89 meV to 41 meV, and to 17 meV in conjunction with standard surface passivation. This interfacial modulation enables inverted perovskite solar cells with a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.2% (stabilized 26.6%) on a 1.02 cm 2 active area. The devices also retain over 98% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of continuous illumination under ambient air conditions. Our work resolves the long-standing puzzle of why C 60 induces severe interfacial recombination and guides the design of comprehensive interface passivation strategies towards efficient perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Nonlinear circular dichroism reveals the local Berry curvature
abstract: The transfer of angular momentum between light and crystalline solids during nonlinear optical processes is typically interpreted in terms of angular momentum conservation and the rotational symmetry of the crystal lattice. However, these cornerstone principles rely on macroscopic symmetry arguments, providing little insight into the microscopic origin of angular momentum transfer. Here we show that changes in the spin angular momentum of light in high-harmonic generation processes, which we probe via nonlinear circular dichroism, are directly proportional to the local Berry curvature at a single optical resonance, therefore establishing a link between nonlinear light–matter interactions and the quantum geometry of electronic states. We demonstrate this relationship using second-harmonic generation in monolayer WSe 2 , using circularly polarized light to break time-reversal symmetry and lift the degeneracy between the valleys. The resulting second-harmonic circular dichroism can be controlled through the intensity and helicity of the circularly polarized light, hence offering a method for the control and readout of the optically probed Berry curvature.

title: Perovskite chiral multiple quantum wells with extended spin lifetime via efficient spin cascade
abstract: The promises of halide perovskites for chiroptical and spintronic applications hinge largely on how long their spin coherence can last. Recent demonstrations of spin injection from chiral single quantum wells to achiral semiconductors have enabled a variety of spin functionalities. However, their spin polarization at the device level remains limited due to rapid interfacial and bulk spin losses. Here we demonstrate a spin cascade strategy by constructing oriented perovskite chiral multiple quantum wells to extend the spin lifetime. In chiral multiple quantum wells, quantum wells with varying well widths exhibit intrinsic and continuous chirality across all quantum-well phases with an average circular dichroism dissymmetry factor of 1.5 × 10 −2 . In this system, slowly energy-varying and spatially coupled chiral multiple quantum wells establish consecutive intermediate polarization states for spin cascade, thereby extending the spin coherence lifetime to ~5 ns at room temperature. The long-lived spin coherence yields circularly polarized luminescence with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (| g lum |) of 1.4 × 10 −2 and spin-dependent charge transport with a polarization degree of over 80%, enabling efficient X-ray-triggered dissymmetric photopolymerization and high-performance circularly polarized light photodetectors. This work opens the way to long-lived spin coherence in halide perovskites, promoting their use in chiroptical and spintronic devices.

title: Controllable transient coherent state reproduction in lasers
abstract: Current research on coherent lasers typically focuses on configurations that maintain a long-term stable state, often ignoring transients during the laser build-up stage. Here we propose and experimentally demonstrate that the transient coherent state (TCS)—occurring during the build-up of laser signals from amplified spontaneous emission in a non-equilibrium long-fibre laser—can be harnessed by periodically resetting the pump power. Using a Fourier-domain mode-locked (FDML) laser as a model, we show that an FDML laser operating in the TCS achieves an instantaneous linewidth at the kilohertz level. This represents a seven-orders-of-magnitude improvement over conventional FDML lasers. Furthermore, the residual phase jitter within the TCS can serve as an internal reference for self-regulation. By leveraging the unique combination of transient coherence and long-term chaos, we demonstrate a novel hybrid light detection and ranging scheme that features micrometre-scale resolution and a kilometre-scale measurable range. Finally, we apply the TCS concept to mitigate multi-longitudinal-mode operation in a self-injection-locked distributed-feedback laser, demonstrating that the TCS is equally valuable for lasers with long-term stable states.

title: Intrinsic backward emission of coherent Raman photons from homogeneous media
abstract: In homogeneous materials, scattered light propagates predominantly in the forward direction; thus, collecting signal on the illumination side often relies on interfaces, disorder or multiple scattering. Nonlinear wave mixing can relax this constraint by combining the directions of the driving fields. If the generated wavelength is longer than the driving wavelengths, intrinsic backward emission can become efficient. Here we exploit this regime using coherent Stokes Raman scattering to generate signal directly into the backward hemisphere. Simulations pinpoint high-numerical aperture geometries and polarization states that maximize backward emission, and experiments confirm backward signals from liquids and tissues with detected levels approaching the strength of forward-detected coherent Raman signals. Because the generated signal originates at the focus and remains refocusable, it enables coherent Raman microscopy with same-side confocal collection compatible with fibre coupling and spectrometers when transmission access is impractical. The approach is particularly relevant and beneficial for samples on opaque substrates, thick specimens, tissue biopsies and fibre- or spectrometer-based implementations.

title: Experimental demonstration of attosecond hard X-ray pulses
abstract: We present the experimental confirmation of attosecond pulse generation in the hard X-ray regime with a free-electron laser. Our experiment is based on the measurements of a nonlinear optical phenomenon known as amplified spontaneous emission from 3 d transition metals. By analysing the yield of the collective X-ray fluorescence induced by ultrashort pulses at the Linac Coherent Light Source, we identify the generation of attosecond pulses and shot-to-shot fluctuations in their duration, ranging from 100 as to 400 as. The inferred time–bandwidth product for 100-as pulses is approximately 2 fs eV, indicating that a fraction of the pulses is nearly transform-limited pulses. Our results confirm the generation of attosecond hard X-ray pulses that can be used to simultaneously probe matter on the timescales of electronic phenomena and with atomic spatial resolution. Furthermore, attosecond hard X-ray pulses can outrun the fastest radiation damage processes, paving the way to single-shot damage-free X-ray measurements.

title: Solution-processed nano-LEDs for next-generation optoelectronic technologies
abstract: Light-emitting diodes (LEDs), with pixel sizes ranging from the millimetre to micrometre scale, have driven advances in display technologies for large-area panels, portable devices and wearable platforms. As applications expand beyond conventional displays to optical sensing, implantable optogenetics, on-chip optical interconnects and super-resolution microscopy, demand is growing for ultracompact, energy-efficient light sources capable of subwavelength and spatiotemporal control. Nanoscale light-emitting diodes (nano-LEDs) stand out as promising candidates to address these requirements, offering exceptional control over light generation, confinement and emission dynamics. Here we discuss recent progress in colloidal quantum dots and perovskite nano-LED technologies across material chemistry, device engineering and nanofabrication strategies. We also propose future research directions for harnessing nano-LEDs in emerging applications, underscoring their potential to move beyond traditional optoelectronic functions. Far beyond a miniaturized extension of conventional LEDs, nano-LEDs are poised to become a transformative platform uniting optoelectronics, nanophotonics and device engineering.

title: Narrow-linewidth, piezoelectrically tunable photonic integrated blue laser
abstract: Frequency-agile lasers operating in the ultraviolet–blue spectral range (360–480 nm) are necessary for a wide range of technologies, including free-space and underwater optical communications, optical atomic clocks, and Rydberg-atom-based quantum computing. Integrated lasers offer a compelling platform for these applications in a compact, robust form factor but remain challenging to realize in this wavelength range. Here we report a photonic integrated blue laser operating at 461 nm, which simultaneously achieves frequency agility and low phase noise. This implementation is based on the hybrid integration of a gallium-nitride-based laser diode, which is self-injection locked to a high- Q microresonator fabricated on a low-loss silicon nitride photonic platform with a propagation loss of ~0.4 dB cm −1 . The laser exhibits a sub-30-kHz linewidth and delivers over 1 mW of optical output power. In addition, aluminium nitride piezoelectric actuators are monolithically integrated onto the photonic circuitry to enable the high-speed modulation of refractive index and allow laser frequency tuning. This enables mode-hop-free laser linear frequency chirps up to 900 MHz at repetition rates up to 1 MHz, with tuning nonlinearity below 2%. We showcase the potential applications of this integrated laser in underwater communication and coherent aerosol sensing experiments.

title: Regulating the crystallization of thermally evaporated perovskites for efficient near-infrared light-emitting diodes
abstract: Thermal evaporation of perovskite films holds considerable promise for the scalable manufacturing and pixel patterning of perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs). However, the performance of evaporated PeLEDs remains inferior to their solution-processed counterparts due to the lack of effective strategies to regulate perovskite crystallization during vacuum deposition. Here we address this challenge and achieve precise control over crystallization pathways. Dual-amide additives suppress premature perovskite phase formation during deposition and decelerate crystallization kinetics during post-annealing. We realize thermally evaporated near-infrared PeLEDs with a maximum external quantum efficiency of 25.0% for emission at 805 nm, and a T 50 lifetime of 23 h at a driving current density of 100 mA cm −2 . To show the advantages of thermal evaporation in pixelization, we realize monolithic dual-colour-emitting PeLEDs at 805 nm and 759 nm by integrating different PeLEDs on the same substrate and demonstrate dual-wavelength wearable pulse oximetry. This work provides insights into vacuum deposition crystallization dynamics and establishes a crystallization regulation methodology to advance evaporated perovskite optoelectronics.

title: Ligand-engineered CsEuI3 nanocrystals for efficient single-component white electroluminescence
abstract: Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) hold notable promise for next-generation full-colour displays. However, realizing full-colour active-matrix displays remains a critical challenge due to varying efficiency across the red, green and blue primary colours and incompatibility with high-resolution patterning techniques. In this context, white PeLEDs paired with colour filters may offer a simplified and efficient alternative to full-colour displays. Here we demonstrate ligand-engineered CsEuI 3 nanocrystals (NCs) that enable efficient single-component white electroluminescence (EL) for full-colour displays. In CsEuI 3 @mCP (mCP: 1,3-bis( N -carbazolyl)benzene) NCs, the intrinsic CsEuI 3 inorganic field preserves blue emission from Eu 2+ , while surface ligand interactions modify the local Eu 2+ environment and introduce complementary long-wavelength emission, producing white emission with a high colour rendering index of 85.7 and near-ideal CIE chromaticity of (0.33, 0.34). Beyond spectral modulation, mCP also promotes the electrical activation of Eu 2+ emissive centres and ligand-assisted excitation involving singlet- and triplet-related states. When implementing CsEuI 3 @mCP NCs as the emitter, we showcase single-component white EL with a peak external quantum efficiency of 8.3% and a maximum luminance of 8,941 cd m −2 . As a proof of concept, we monolithically integrate these white PeLEDs on a 256 × 256 active-matrix display chip, demonstrating dynamic video and full-colour images with a 124% NTSC colour gamut. This work establishes ligand engineering as a strategy for coupling electrical activation with spectral modulation in rare-earth electroluminescent materials.

title: Low-voltage avalanche heterojunction phototransistor for infrared-to-visible upconversion
abstract: Converting low-energy, invisible photons to high-energy, visible photons represents a considerable challenge for essential applications in photonics such as night vision, medical imaging and optogenetics. Although nonlinear optical processes are commonly used for such upconversion, they often suffer from low efficiency and require bulk optical crystals and strong optical pumping. A promising solid-state approach to achieving upconversion is to detect low-energy photons with a high-gain photodetector made from a narrow-bandgap semiconductor, which generates sufficient photocurrent to drive a visible-light LED. However, previous attempts have struggled to meet the stringent requirements of infrared sensitivity, high gain and low driving voltage simultaneously. Here we demonstrate that an intrinsic gain feedback mechanism in an InGaAs/InP avalanche heterojunction phototransistor can power an amber-light LED, making it over 17,000 times brighter than the input infrared light at an incident intensity of just 6.4 nW cm − 2 , close to the nightglow level. The phototransistor is uniquely engineered to feature an internal positive feedback loop between its transistor amplification and avalanche gain, resulting in a breakdown voltage as low as 1.4 V and enabling an avalanche upconversion mode with ultrahigh conversion efficiency. Our results highlight the potential of solid-state solutions for wearable, direct-view night vision and establish a general and scalable pathway for photon upconversion across a broad infrared spectral range.

title: Deep subwavelength laser nanofabrication via upconversion
abstract: Three-dimensional laser nanofabrication has revolutionized the creation of functional micro/nanostructures for use in biomedicine, communications, energy and sensing devices. Yet conventional strategies face critical trade-offs in terms of resolution, scalability and cost. In contrast, upconversion laser nanofabrication (UC-LN) leverages nonlinear photon management in upconversion materials to decouple fabrication resolution from the laser source constraints, offering both structural programmability and functional customization. By converting near-infrared light into localized high-energy emissions, UC-LN enables deep subwavelength 3D nanofabrication at lower continuous-wave excitation intensities, circumventing the need for high-cost femtosecond lasers. Here we describe the principles and benefits of UC-LN, highlight its versatility in fabricating highly customizable architectures, and discuss emerging applications and the key challenges that lie ahead for the technology. We also propose innovative strategies to establish UC-LN as a viable and scalable alternative for next-generation 3D nanomanufacturing.

title: Automatic on-chip separation of partially coherent light into its mutually incoherent components
abstract: While partial coherence often degrades interference and information transfer, its correlations can be engineered to enhance imaging and optical information processing. However, approaches based on tomography and numerical reconstruction do not physically separate unknown fields into their coherence modes—that is, their orthogonal and mutually incoherent components. Here we demonstrate the separation of partially coherent light into coherence modes. We use variational processing in layered self-configuring interferometers on a silicon photonic circuit. This process finds the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the coherency matrix, characterizing the state while leaving it intact and separated after optimization. We show that spatially orthogonal, mutually incoherent beams can be routed to separate outputs even when their intensity profiles overlap. Our experiment separates the two strongest coherence modes from a nine-input sampling of overlapping fields from two independent lasers; operation beyond two modes is verified in a rank-3 experiment. The number of physical components scales linearly with the rank r of the coherency matrix, through r in situ gradient-based optimizations enabled by electronic drive-frequency multiplexing of the phase shifters. We benchmark performance against an on-chip mixture-based tomographic method. These results establish a scalable framework for programmable coherence analysis and control.

title: Infrared polymer boasts high index and transparency
abstract: A bifunctional cyano-substitution synthetic strategy yields an all-organic polymer with a record-breaking refractive index of 2.53 at 750 nm, combining high infrared transparency with mechanical flexibility and solution-processability.

title: Workhorse solid-state lasers reinvented
abstract: Miniature versions of famous bulk solid-state sources, notably titanium–sapphire and Nd:YAG lasers, have now become a reality. This advance has been made possible through collaborative efforts from material science, heterogeneous integration and fabrication technologies.

title: Measuring hard X-ray attosecond pulses
abstract: The generation and characterization of high-power X-ray attosecond pulses is a challenging research frontier in free-electron laser science. Now, researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source have demonstrated experimental confirmation and measurement of hard X-ray pulses reaching 100-attosecond durations.

title: Femtosecond lasers drive nanostructuring and green applications
abstract: From ultra-precise nanofabrication to sustainable use cases, femtosecond lasers continue to expand their application potential.

title: Optical control stabilizes cold-atom comagnetometry
abstract: The use of tailored laser fields improves the coherence times of two co-trapped ytterbium isotopes, resulting in the rejection of magnetic-field noise by more than thirty-thousand-fold, opening the way to improved comagnetometry.

title: Light-switch for nerve cells
Pure-blue quantum-dot light-emitting diodes with minimal efficiency roll-off and high brightness
abstract: Quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs) are promising candidates for augmented reality, virtual reality and other high-resolution microdisplay applications. For these applications, the QLEDs must sustain high efficiency at high luminance while remaining compatible with device-integration processes. However, blue QLEDs still face pronounced efficiency roll-off and processing-related performance degradation. Here we develop pure-blue-emitting quantum dots based on a CdZnSe core with a compositionally graded ZnSe/ZnSeS/ZnS shell, combined with ZnCl 2 -assisted surface morphology modulation. This design suppresses surface-trap-related recombination and improves processing robustness. We demonstrate bottom-emission QLEDs at 464 nm with a peak external quantum efficiency of 23.8% and a 95% external quantum efficiency retention at 50,000 cd m −2 ( L 95 ). The top-emission QLEDs reached L 95 = 270,000 cd m −2 and a blue index of 586. We also demonstrate patterned QLEDs via photolithography with a resolution of 560 pixels per inch and peak external quantum efficiency of 16.5%. Our results demonstrate pure-blue quantum-dot emitters that combine Rec. 2020-near emission, minimal efficiency roll-off at high brightness, compatibility with direct photolithographic patterning and top-emission device integration for advanced display applications.
